div.p: Burst error model describes phenomena which cause potentially random faults over a bounded time interval. We study the worst response time for tasks under fixed-priority with checkpoints. Since checkpointing schemes depend on time redundancy, they could affect the correctness of the system by causing deadlines to be missed. In this paper, we provide an exact schedulability analysis for burst error model and derive the optimal number of checkpoints. We also explore the faulttolerant priority assignment policy to get the most efficient scheme.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Fault tolerance is the property which enables a system to continue with its correct operation even in the presence of errors [1] . To provide fault-tolerant systems is usually designed so that some redundancy is included. In some limited space and weight application such as space missions, hardware redundancy are limited and time redundancy becomes essential [2] . Time redundancy is employed in the form of recovery blocks, re-execution of the affected task or checkpointing and rollback recovery.

Checkpointing is a relatively cost effective method for achieving fault-tolerant in real-time systems, which has been the focus of research for a long time. Unlike reexecution schemes, checkpointing recovery errors by making use of previously saved state of the task, which consists of values of data variables and contents of system registers. During the execution of a task, the system saves task's state in a reliable storage facility, it is crucial that each checkpoint is error-free, and this can be done by running acceptance tests to validate the correctness of the checkpoint. When a fault is detected, the system rolls back to the most previously stored state and resumes normal execution. Checkpointing enables a reduction in the recovery time from a fault by saving intermediate states of a task in a stable storage device. The number of checkpoints affects the worst case execution time of the task. Whereas inserting more checkpoints and reduce the interval between them reduces the reprocessing time after faults.

Schedulability analysis is mainly based on the relation of the task worst-case response time and its deadline. When worst-case response time is earlier than the deadline, the system is schedulable. Otherwise, the system is unschedulable. The error pattern must be known to establish an efficient schedulability analysis of fault tolerance. Usually, researcher analysis a given worst-case scenario for fault model and then adjust feasibility analysis to check if a given system is schedulable when subject to a given error pattern. Pseudo-periodic model represents a fault distribution that two consecutive faults are separated by a minimum time interval which is a classic fault model in real-time system. This fault model is effective to manage either punctual faults or disturbances caused by electromagnetic compatibility; but it cannot be effective management of phenomena that cause potentially random faults over a bounded time interval [3] . This situation is commonly found in sensor obstacles or airport landing gear aircraft on the radar wave [14] . Burst error model can be a very good description of this phenomenon.

In this paper, we present schedulability analysis for checkpointing schemes based on worst-case response time. These schedulability analysis tests present that checkpointing can offer reliability and real-time guarantees under fault bursts models. We also calculate the optimal number of checkpoints for each task. The optimal number of checkpoints can help the task to minimize the worst case execution time in the presence of faults. Under this scheme, we consider the recovery of lower priority tasks running with higher priorities. Also, we show that these policies may improve the system fault resilience.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:The next section presents the assumed computation model and burst error model. Then, we give the main motivation by presenting an illustrative example in Section 3. Section 4 provides the schedulability analysis for checkpointing schema under burst error model and derive the optimal number of checkpoints. In section 5, the method to finding out the optimal fault-tolerant priority configuration is given.

div.head: Burst Error Model
div.p: We assume in the paper that the burst error model represents a time interval ∆F in which the fault distribution is unknown, and there is a minimum time between two fault burst. No fault can occur outside ∆F. The minimum time interval between two consecutive faults in a fault burst is unknown. Consequently, ∆F is considered as a black box which causes faults on task sets during the fault burst. The burst error model is drawn in Figure 1. The following hypothesis is an assumption in fault tolerance scheduling. T F is greater than equal to the greatest task deadline of the task set. We assume that system has an instantaneous update rate. No reset or restart is necessary to have the nominal behaviour of the system. Therefore, at the end of a fault burst, system recovers its nominal behaviour.The maximum value of ∆F is an important information about the system's fault resilience. We attribute ∆F to a standard of the ability to tolerate faults.

div.p: F i is the recovery term which is included error detections and error corrections. Different equation of the term F i according to the error recovery strategies be mentioned by reference [3]. There are two kinds of error recovery strategy, distinguish by the scheduler behavior after a fault is detected; named simple strategy(ED/FR/S) and multiple strategy(ED/FR/M). Simple strategy means that only the faulty task is re-execution when an error is detected.In a multiple strategy, if an error is detected in a task the scheduler applies an error correction to the current task,then interrupts all preempted tasks and executes an error correction on each of them.

For these two strategies, error correction is based on reexecution of task, so the error recovery term is the multiples of the execution time of tasks. This is against to the system's fault resilience. It can be seen that the schedulability of a task set under faults can be improved if we reduce the additionnal computation time requirement after the fault occurrence. In the case where we resort to re-execution of the task, the system needs the same amount of execution time upon a fault. If we employ checkpoint, we need to execute the task only after the last checkpoint which considerably reduces the additional computation requirement upon fault occurrence. div.p: While calculate the response time, the overhead caused by checkpoint can be divided into two parts:one part is the inevitable checkpointing overhead which is dependent on system's parameters, and the other part of the overhead is the recovery of executions. They are closely related to the number of checkpoints. When a large number of checkpoints are used, the overhead caused by checkpointing increases due to that the checkpointing operations will be performed more frequently. At the same time when a large number of checkpoints is used, the overhead due to recovery is reduced due to the fact that the length of the execution segments is reduced. But when a low number of checkpoints are used, the overhead due to checkpointing decreases, due to that the checkpointing operations will be performed less frequently. At the same time, when a low number of checkpoints is used, the overhead due to recovery increases, due to that the length of the execution segments is increased. So we must find out the optimal number of checkpoints.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: This section characterizes the applicability of the described approach by simulation. We compare the error recovery strategies under differernt processor utilization.

For a given processor utilization, 1000 task sets (5 tasks per task set) were generated. All the task set are schedulable under the no-failure hypothesis. The periods and deadlines of tasks were assigned according to a uniform distribution with minimum and maximum values set to 10 and 100, respectively. Deadlines were allowed to be less than or equal to periods. We used the deadline monotonic algorithm to assign the priorities of task.

The correction of strategy is worked by a full re-execution of the erroneous task. Second, we propose the schedulability analysis under burst error model for checkpoint schemes and derive the optimal number of checkpoints to improve system fault resilience. The example shows that the optimal checkpoint scheme is more efficiently. Furthermore, we dealt with fault-tolerant priority assignment policy. We introduced the fault-tolerant priority configuration algorithm that brings into account the fact that the recoveries of tasks may be executed at high priority levels. The proposed algorithm could improve system fault resilience when the two former approaches cannot do it. This is demonstrated by our illustration example and evaluation.
